https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/LibreSSL
Libre ssl is a fork of open ssl that was created after the heartbleed bug a little while a go, open ssl is the more popular version with more developers and funding behind it.
Which is why is so open to backdoors.

OpenSSL is free software meaning anybody can do pretty much anything they want with it. LibreSSL is a fork of that. A fork is essentially copying a project in its entirety, declaring it a new project and beginning to perform typically radical changes to it that might not necessarily be appropriate in the original project. Google also forked OpenSSL to create BoringSSL.

OpenSSL, in spite of its huge relevance, was maintained by a small number of developers who were reportedly not particularly responsive to feedback or bug reports. The code itself was also horribly bloated and unwieldy. LibreSSL claimed to have simply wiped something like 90,000 lines of code within the first week - or about 25% of the entire code base! However, in the process of this huge level of refactoring they themselves have created enormous numbers of exploits and vulnerabilities. In the longrun it could be good, but it's not going to be replacing OpenSSL any time soon.

In my opinion the one of the biggest issues is the language the library is written in: C. It's a great language, but in projects of substantial complexity it's all but impossible to maintain complete security. There's just too many ways to shoot yourself in the foot. It's also not exactly the most readable language which is another major issue for maintenance and security in a large scale project. This is made even worse by developers who seem to think it's cool to use terrible naming conventions. For instance here is the heartbleed code:

*bp++ = TLS1_HB_RESPONSE;
s2n(payload, bp);
memcpy(bp, pl, payload);

Variable names bp, pl. Functions named s2n (and a sister function named n2s) and so on. Have fun having any clue whatsoever the code is doing (even if you wrote it!) when you see code like that a few months later, let alone having hundreds of thousands of lines of this mess.

Actually, the number of bugs has been rather small. And though they have introduced bugs, those have generally been on the portable versions of the codebase rather than on the OpenBSD-specific development version. The major cause for created bugs through this move from OpenBSD to portable has been the assumptions made with regards to functions on other systems. The people do the coding were expecting things to work how they are familiar with them rather than investigating all the differing ways functions work with each library.

I find that as the time has gone on their enthusiasm has waned but they are still going at it at a rather fast pace.

They are already beginning to use it as the default TLS/SSL solution on OpenBSD, there is going to be a ports hackathon where they try converting over as many as possible to start putting it through a real work out.
